task_title: Aircraft Flight Controls and Operation of Systems
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain every system on your training airplane, from the flight controls to oxygen, at commercial-pilot depth, teach each one with the POH and the airplane itself, spot and fix the systems errors students make, and coach a pilot through a system failure or into an unfamiliar airplane or avionics suite.
why: Students who only memorize a systems section cannot answer a question the book did not cover; a learner who understands how a system works can handle unfamiliar aircraft and new avionics [[25:61|AIH 3-10]]. As the instructor you also carry your own systems hazard: any unfamiliarity with the aircraft, avionics or procedures you teach in creates a hazard [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. This Task tests both, on the airplane you bring to the checkride (ACS AI.II.E objective).

prereading.what: Primary and secondary flight controls, every kind of tab, and the autopilot. Short; read all of it.
prereading.label: PHAK 6-1 to 6-12

prereading.what: Engine, propeller, induction, ignition, oil, cooling, fuel, heat, electrical, hydraulics, landing gear, pressurization, oxygen and ice protection. Skip the turbine pages.
prereading.label: PHAK 7-1 to 7-42

prereading.what: Pitot-static system, blockages and the alternate static source, the PFD and AHRS, and the vacuum system.
prereading.label: PHAK 8-2 to 8-16

prereading.what: Automation: TAA, over-reliance, information management, mode awareness and why humans monitor poorly.
prereading.label: PHAK 2-25 to 2-31

prereading.what: Electrical fire, flap and elevator failures, gear malfunction, electrical and pitot-static failures, glass display failures and the abnormal engine indication table.
prereading.label: AFH 18-10 to 18-16

prereading.what: Demonstration-performance, telling-and-doing, positive exchange of controls, and managing risk when you instruct, including your own unfamiliarity.
prereading.label: AIH 9-5 to 9-9, 10-5 to 10-7

prereading.what: Transition to unfamiliar aircraft: the systems study list, the flow method, checklists, procedure categories and the blindfold test.
prereading.label: AC 90-109A para 8

warmup: Think first: your student can recite the fuel system page of the POH word for word. On the ramp you point at the fuel selector and ask, "What happens to the fuel after it leaves here, and how would you know if it stopped?" She has no answer. What did memorizing miss, and how would you teach that system differently next time?

key_terms.def: Ailerons, elevator (or stabilator) and rudder: the controls required to control the airplane safely in flight [[1:150|PHAK 6-2]].
Wing flaps, leading edge devices, spoilers and trim systems. They improve performance or relieve the pilot of excessive control forces [[1:150|PHAK 6-2]].
Yaw toward the raised wing, opposite the direction of bank, caused by the extra drag of the down aileron [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]].
A tab on a stabilator that moves in the same direction as its trailing edge, making the stabilator less sensitive and also acting as a trim device [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]].
A controllable-pitch propeller whose governor changes blade angle in flight to hold the rpm the pilot selects [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]].
A common terminal that connects the main electrical system to the equipment that uses electricity [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].
A gauge that starts at zero and shows the load on the alternator or generator as a share of its capacity [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].
A static source, usually inside the flight deck, used when the primary static source is blocked [[1:204|PHAK 8-2]].
Attitude and heading reference system. It feeds the attitude display and, with the magnetometer, the heading display on a PFD [[1:215|PHAK 8-13]].
The demonstrated ability to control and navigate the airplane with its automated systems, including knowing when to use them and when not to [[25:23|AIH 1-19]].

Studying a system by following what moves through it, for example fuel from the filler port to the cylinder, or current from the battery to the bus to each appliance [[57:15|AC 90-109A para 8b]] [[57:16|AC 90-109A para 8b(2)]].
A procedure for a system that is not working properly but is not threatening, such as an electric trim failure; after it, workload should rise only slightly [[57:17|AC 90-109A para 8c(3)(b)]].

chunks.title: Teaching systems: the POH, the airplane, and understanding

body.p: This Task covers the flight controls and systems of the airplane you bring to the checkride, and the examiner checks that you can also provide effective instruction on them (ACS AI.II.E objective). If the examiner selects K1, all of its sub-elements must be assessed (ACS AI.II.E note). So know every system on your airplane, not just your favorite three.

The handbooks describe typical systems only. Because flight controls and systems vary so much between aircraft, the primary source for the airplane you fly is its AFM or POH [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]] [[1:202|PHAK 7-42]]. Teach your students to open the POH first, every time.

Aim for understanding, not recitation. The AIH describes three phases of knowledge: memorization, understanding and application [[25:60|AIH 3-9]]. Its example is the mixture control: a learner who only memorized the steps cannot say what happens if the mixture is too rich or too lean, but one who knows that combustion needs a certain fuel-air ratio and that air thins with altitude can [[25:60|AIH 3-9]] [[25:61|AIH 3-10]]. Learners who understand a process also master variations of it more easily, such as unfamiliar aircraft and new avionics [[25:61|AIH 3-10]].

bullets: Teach each system as a flow. Follow what moves through it: fuel from the filler port, through the tank, selector and pump, to the carburetor or injectors; current from the battery and alternator to the buses to the appliances; control inputs from the cockpit through the linkages to the surface [[57:15|AC 90-109A para 8b]] [[57:16|AC 90-109A para 8b(2)]].
Use the flow to explain normal, abnormal and emergency procedures, and to make the preflight inspection better at finding unsafe conditions [[57:16|AC 90-109A para 8b(3)]].
Draw it. Schematics and diagrams make the relationship between subsystems easy to see [[25:127|AIH 5-24]].
Pair the ground lesson with the airplane. Ground and flight instruction belong together, and the learner advances further and faster that way [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

Use the cockpit itself: have the learner sit in the airplane until every control can be found without searching, and use a blindfold drill where you call out controls and switches [[57:44|AC 90-109A App 7]].

callout.text: Ask "why" and "what if" questions, not "what is" questions. "What happens to the ammeter if the alternator quits?" shows understanding; "How many volts is the system?" only shows memory (application of [[25:60|AIH 3-9]]).

check.q: Name three teaching tools the sources give for systems, besides lecture.
check.a: Any three: the flow method [[57:15|AC 90-109A para 8b]], schematics and diagrams [[25:127|AIH 5-24]], sitting in the airplane and the blindfold drill [[57:44|AC 90-109A App 7]], and pairing ground with flight lessons [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

body.p: Primary flight controls are the ailerons, elevator or stabilator, and rudder [[1:150|PHAK 6-2]]. In a small airplane they are usually mechanical: rods, cables, pulleys and sometimes chains carry the pilot's input to the surfaces [[1:149|PHAK 6-1]]. Control stops limit how far the surfaces can move, so the pilot cannot easily overcontrol and overstress the airplane [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]].

head: Surface
What it does
Teaching point
rows: Ailerons
Roll about the longitudinal axis. Wheel right: right aileron up, left aileron down, airplane rolls right [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]]
Adverse yaw: the down aileron adds drag, so the nose yaws away from the turn. It grows at low airspeed and with large aileron deflection [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]] [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]]
Elevator
Pitch about the lateral axis. Aft column raises the trailing edge, the tail moves down and the nose up [[1:153|PHAK 6-5]]
An elevator down spring may be installed to lower the nose if an aft-CG airplane slows [[1:154|PHAK 6-6]]
Stabilator
A one-piece tail that pivots on a central hinge; very sensitive, so an antiservo tab adds feel [[1:155|PHAK 6-7]]
Show the antiservo tab moving with the trailing edge on the walkaround [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]]
Rudder
Yaw about the vertical axis. Left pedal moves the rudder left and the nose left [[1:156|PHAK 6-8]]
Rudder gets more effective with speed and slipstream, so large inputs are needed when slow [[1:156|PHAK 6-8]]

body.p: Coordinated turns use all three. Aileron sets the bank, rudder cancels adverse yaw, and back pressure adds the extra lift needed in the turn; rudder needed is greatest at low airspeed, high angle of attack and large aileron deflection [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]]. Designers reduce adverse yaw with differential ailerons, Frise-type ailerons, coupled aileron and rudder, and flaperons, but none removes it entirely [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]]. Rudder-aileron interconnect springs can be overridden when you need to slip [[1:153|PHAK 6-5]].

How to teach it on the ground: walk the airplane and have the learner move the wheel while you watch each surface, and name which way each one moves and why. Do a full range of motion check and verify that each surface moves freely and in the correct direction; on some light-sport airplanes the down aileron moves very little by design [[24:344|AFH 17-10]]. Before that, the control lock must be removed [[24:42|AFH 2-5]]. Tell the story of the Boeing 299: a highly experienced crew tried to take off with the controls locked, which is why checklists became standard [[57:16|AC 90-109A para 8c]].

How to show it in flight: when you demonstrate a turn, explain that aileron deflection sets the roll rate and how long it is held sets the bank angle, then neutralize and trim [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. A student who does not know this keeps holding aileron and overbanks.

callout.text: Controls feel soft and respond slowly at low airspeed and get firm and quick at high airspeed [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]]. Point this out during slow flight, so the learner does not mistake mushy controls for a malfunction, or big low-speed inputs for good technique at cruise.

check.q: Your student rolls into a left turn with aileron alone at slow speed. Which way does the nose start to go, and what fixes it?
check.a: Right, away from the turn, because the down aileron on the right wing adds drag (adverse yaw). Left rudder with the aileron fixes it, and more is needed at low airspeed [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]] [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]].

chunks.title: Secondary flight controls: flaps, spoilers and trim

body.p: Secondary flight controls are wing flaps, leading edge devices, spoilers and trim systems [[1:156|PHAK 6-8]]. Flaps increase both lift and induced drag at a given angle of attack; the four common types are plain, split, slotted and Fowler [[1:156|PHAK 6-8]]. Flap extension can pitch the nose up or down depending on the airplane, which the pilot usually corrects with trim [[1:157|PHAK 6-9]].

bullets: Flaps: up to about 15 degrees mostly add lift with little drag; beyond 15 degrees drag rises sharply, and most high-wing airplanes pitch nose-up [[24:233|AFH 12-2]].
Use the same flap setting at the same point in every pattern, so a go-around is a familiar, preplanned sequence [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].
Never exceed the AFM/POH flap setting for takeoff [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].
Leading edge devices (fixed slots, movable slats, leading edge flaps, cuffs) delay separation and raise the maximum lift coefficient [[1:157|PHAK 6-9]] [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]].
Spoilers spoil lift and add drag; used for roll control they eliminate adverse yaw [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]].

head: Trim device
How it moves
What to tell the student
rows: Elevator trim tab
Opposite the elevator. Full nose-down trim puts the tab full up, which pushes the elevator trailing edge down [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]]
If you hold steady back pressure, you need nose-up trim [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]]
Balance tab
Automatically opposite the surface, to lighten control forces [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]]
It is not a trim unless its linkage is adjustable from the cockpit [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]]
Antiservo tab
Same direction as the stabilator trailing edge; adds feel and also trims [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]]
Point it out on a stabilator airplane during the walkaround
Ground adjustable tab
A metal tab on the rudder bent on the ground until the airplane stops skidding in cruise [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]] [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]]
It is set on the ground by trial and error, never in flight
Adjustable stabilizer
The whole stabilizer pivots on a jackscrew; same effect as a trim tab [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]]
Same cockpit control and indication as a trim tab [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]]

body.p: The trim procedure to teach: set power, pitch attitude and configuration first, then trim off the control pressure, and retrim whenever power, pitch or configuration changes [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]] [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]]. On airplanes with electric trim, the preflight should include running the trim both ways, checking the trim disconnect, and setting takeoff trim; the pilot must know how to respond to a trim runaway [[24:344|AFH 17-10]].

callout.text: Configuration and trim changes are a classic distraction. Preoccupation inside the flight deck while changing configuration or trim can set up a stall or spin [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Teach eyes outside and attitude held while the flaps move.

check.q: A learner flies the climb by rolling the trim wheel to raise and lower the nose. What is wrong, and what do you teach instead?
check.a: Trim is not for changing attitude. Set the attitude, power and configuration with the controls first, then trim to relieve the pressure, and retrim after each change [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]] [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]].

body.p: Powerplant and propeller: most small airplanes have four-stroke, spark-ignition, horizontally opposed, air-cooled engines [[1:162|PHAK 7-2]] [[1:163|PHAK 7-3]]. Teach the engine as several systems working together: induction, ignition, fuel, oil, cooling and exhaust all have to work for the engine to keep running [[1:164|PHAK 7-4]].

head: Item
Key facts
How students get it wrong
rows: Ignition
Two independent magnetos each fire one of two plugs per cylinder; they need no aircraft electrical power [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]] [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]
Thinking master OFF makes the propeller safe. With the ignition on, a moved propeller can start the engine [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]
Mag check
A small rpm drop on each magneto is normal; the allowed drop is in the AFM/POH. Too much drop, or no drop, means do not fly [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]] [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]
Treating "no drop" as a perfect result
Mixture
Air thins with altitude while fuel density stays the same, so the mixture gets richer; lean it with the mixture control. A too-lean mixture can cause detonation [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]
Leaning by habit, not by the AFM/POH procedure for that airplane [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]
Carburetor ice

Most likely below 70 degrees F with humidity above 80 percent, but possible up to 100 degrees F and 50 percent [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]. Fixed pitch: rpm drops first. Constant speed: manifold pressure drops, rpm holds [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Using partial heat, or taking heat off when the engine runs rough as the ice melts [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Constant-speed prop
Throttle sets manifold pressure, the propeller control sets rpm [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]]. To reduce power, manifold pressure first; to increase, rpm first [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]]
Pulling rpm back first, which raises manifold pressure and can overstress the cylinders [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]]
Cooling
Air cooling is weakest at high power and low airspeed. Lower CHT by adding airspeed, enriching the mixture or reducing power, or with cowl flaps [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]] [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]]
Long steep climbs at full power on a hot day

body.p: Teaching point: the mixture control is the AIH's own example of teaching for understanding. Once the learner knows why the mixture gets rich as the air thins, questions like "what if it is too lean in the descent?" answer themselves [[25:61|AIH 3-10]]. Do the same with carburetor ice: draw the venturi, show where the temperature drops, and let the learner predict where the ice forms [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

callout.text: On the run-up, have the learner say what each check proves before doing it: the mag check proves both ignition paths, the carb heat check proves the heat source works [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]] [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]].

check.q: Your learner in a constant-speed airplane asks why the tachometer never warned her of carburetor ice. What do you explain?
check.a: The governor changes blade pitch to hold the selected rpm, so carb ice shows as a drop in manifold pressure with no rpm change [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

bullets: Landing gear: tricycle gear lets you brake harder without nosing over, improves forward visibility, and resists ground loops because the CG is ahead of the main wheels [[1:193|PHAK 7-33]].
Tailwheel gear puts the CG behind the mains, so a swerve can grow into a ground loop, and forward visibility is poor; that is why specific training is required [[1:194|PHAK 7-34]].

Nosewheels are steerable or castering; with a castering nosewheel the pilot may need differential braking along with the rudder [[1:193|PHAK 7-33]]. Brakes are on the main wheels and the toe or heel pedals work independently [[1:194|PHAK 7-34]].
Retractable gear may be mechanical, hydraulic, electric or a mix, and the pilot must know the system, including emergency extension [[57:51|AC 90-109A App 10]].

Hydraulic system (the hydraulic part of K1e): a reservoir, a pump, a filter, a selector valve, a relief valve and an actuator. In small airplanes it often works the brakes, retractable gear and some constant-speed propellers [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].
Service it only with the hydraulic fluid the manufacturer specifies [[1:193|PHAK 7-33]].

body.p: Teaching the gear on the ground: start with the gear position in the POH preflight. In a retractable airplane, the gear handle must be confirmed DOWN before the master switch goes on, and the down-and-locked lights are checked green [[24:42|AFH 2-5]]. Then trace the hydraulic flow on the POH schematic from the pump to the actuator and back, using the flow method [[57:16|AC 90-109A para 8b(3)]].

callout.text: If a gear leg will not come down by the normal or alternate POH methods, plan a gear-up landing at an airport with crash and rescue equipment, and ask for it to stand by [[24:361|AFH 18-12]].

check.q: Why do tailwheel airplanes require specific training?
check.a: The CG is behind the main gear, which makes ground directional control harder and can lead to a ground loop, and forward visibility is reduced near the ground [[1:194|PHAK 7-34]].

chunks.title: Fuel and oil: teach it as a flow

body.p: Fuel system: it must deliver an uninterrupted flow of clean fuel to the engine in every approved attitude and power setting. Small airplanes use gravity-feed systems (high wing, tanks above the carburetor) or fuel-pump systems (low wing), and pump systems have an engine-driven pump plus an electric auxiliary or boost pump [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]].

head: Flow step
Questions to ask the learner (AC 90-109A)
Facts to teach
rows: Filler port
What fuel, what color, how many ports? [[57:15|AC 90-109A para 8b]]
Never use a lower grade than required; 100LL is blue, Jet A is clear or straw [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]]
Tank
How many tanks? Where are the drains? How is quantity shown? [[57:15|AC 90-109A para 8b]]
Gauges must be accurate only at empty, so check tanks visually [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]]. Tanks are vented [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]]
Selector valve
Can you find and work it by feel? Which tank for takeoff and landing? [[57:15|AC 90-109A para 8b]]
Running a tank dry can let air in and cause vapor lock [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]]
Pickup, pump, strainer
Is there an electric pump, when is it on, how do you know it works? [[57:16|AC 90-109A para 8b]]
Drain the strainer before each flight; keep draining if you find water [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]] [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]]
Carburetor or injectors
How is mixture controlled? When is carb heat used? [[57:16|AC 90-109A para 8b]]
Lock the primer, or it can vibrate out and richen the mixture [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]]

body.p: Fuel mismanagement matters: complex and high-performance airplanes can have complicated fuel systems, and the AC cites a report that almost one-third of fuel-related accidents came from fuel mismanagement [[57:51|AC 90-109A App 10]]. An NTSB case in the same AC shows a pilot who lost control while reaching for an unmarked, awkwardly placed fuel selector [[57:43|AC 90-109A App 7]] [[57:44|AC 90-109A App 7]].

Oil (the oil part of K1e) lubricates, cools by reducing friction, removes cylinder heat, seals the pistons and carries away contaminants [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]. Oil pressure should show during the start; oil temperature rises slowly, and a high reading may mean a plugged line, low oil, a blocked cooler or a bad gauge [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]] [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].

callout.text: Fuel flow: port, tank, selector, then the strainer and pumps (their order varies; Figure 7-30 shows the strainer before the pumps), then the carburetor or injectors. Have the learner trace it with a finger on the POH diagram, then on the airplane [[57:15|AC 90-109A para 8b]].

check.q: Your student's first fuel strainer sample shows water. What next?
check.a: Drain more samples until no trace appears; water can still remain in the tanks, which only the tank sump drains remove [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]].

body.p: Electrical system: most airplanes have a 14- or 28-volt DC system: alternator or generator, battery, master or battery switch, alternator switch, bus bar with fuses and circuit breakers, voltage regulator, ammeter or loadmeter, and wiring [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]. The master switch powers everything except the ignition system [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].

bullets: With the alternator half of a split master switch OFF, the whole load falls on the battery; turn off everything nonessential [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].
Ammeter: plus shows the battery charging; minus means more is drawn than replaced. Full-scale minus points to the alternator, full-scale plus to the regulator [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].
Loadmeter: shows the load on the alternator; with everything off it shows only the battery's charging current [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].
The regulator keeps alternator output above battery voltage, about 14 volts for a 12-volt battery [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].
Circuit breakers do the job of fuses but can be reset; placards name each circuit and its amperage [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].

body.p: How to teach it: trace the current from the battery and alternator to the buses to each appliance, the way the AC describes [[57:16|AC 90-109A para 8b(2)]]. Then ask flow questions: "If the alternator field breaker pops, what still works and for how long?" A learner who can answer that from the schematic understands the system.

callout.text: Electrically powered gear and flaps draw far more current than most equipment. Selecting them on a partly drained battery may cause an immediate total loss of electrical power [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

check.q: With all electrical equipment off, the loadmeter still shows a small load. What is it?
check.a: The charging current the battery is demanding [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].

body.p: Avionics: a technically advanced airplane typically has a PFD, an MFD with an instrument-certified GPS showing traffic and terrain, and an integrated autopilot [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]. On a PFD, the attitude display comes from the AHRS and the heading from a magnetometer feeding the AHRS; engine data such as the tachometer is usually on the MFD and moves to the remaining screen if a display fails [[1:215|PHAK 8-13]].

head: Skill (PHAK)
What it means
How you teach it
rows: Information management
Understand the system at a conceptual level, then stop, look and read before pushing, pulling or twisting [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]]
Have the learner explain the page structure before touching a knob; use simulation software and the system manual [[25:22|AIH 1-18]]
Automation management
Know at all times which modes are engaged and which are armed, and verify armed modes engage [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]
Require a callout after every mode change or arming [[25:23|AIH 1-19]]
Risk management
Lighter workload can bring complacency; humans monitor automation poorly [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]
Warn the learner about the passive-monitor trap and build habits that keep attention focused [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]

body.p: The instructor's goal is a learner who can fly with all the available automation and also knows how and when to fly without it; no one level of automation suits every situation [[25:23|AIH 1-19]]. Pilots who relied on automation lost manual skill, so pilots of automated aircraft should occasionally disengage it and hand fly [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]]. Over-reliance on automated flight systems has caused accidents [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10]].

Know how the autopilot interacts with the rest of the system. On some autopilots, switching the HSI source from GPS to LOC or VOR while in NAV mode drops NAV mode and the autopilot reverts to wing leveling until the pilot re-engages it [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. Autopilots can be manually overridden and have a disconnect [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]].

callout.text: Plan with the learner, on the ground, when and where programming will be done and when it will not, for example no reprogramming below a set altitude [[25:22|AIH 1-18]].

check.q: At the most basic level, what does managing the autopilot mean?
check.a: Knowing at all times which modes are engaged and which are armed, and verifying the armed modes engage when they should [[25:23|AIH 1-19]] [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

body.p: Pitot-static system and its flight instruments: the pitot tube senses total pressure through a front opening and has a drain hole at the back; static ports sense ambient pressure. The airspeed indicator uses both; the altimeter and VSI use static only [[1:204|PHAK 8-2]].

head: Failure
What the student sees
Fix to teach
rows: Pitot blocked, drain open
Airspeed falls to zero [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]
Pitot heat in visible moisture, per the AFM/POH [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]
Pitot and drain blocked
Airspeed acts like an altimeter: rises in a climb, falls in a descent [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]
Do not chase it; use pitch and power
Static blocked
Altimeter freezes, VSI shows zero, airspeed wrong [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]
Open the alternate static source [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]
Static partly blocked
Normal in the climb; in the descent too high, too fast and descending slowly [[24:363|AFH 18-14]] [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]
Open the alternate static in a climb or descent; if the needles jump, keep it open [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]

body.p: With the alternate static source in use, the altimeter reads slightly high, the airspeed reads high, and the VSI shows a momentary climb [[1:205|PHAK 8-3]]. Without one, breaking the VSI glass is a last-resort way to let static pressure in [[1:205|PHAK 8-3]]. In many glass-cockpit light airplanes the backup instruments share the same pitot-static inputs as the PFD, so a blockage can take out both [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

Vacuum/pressure system: an engine-driven vacuum pump pulls air through a filter and the attitude and heading indicators; a relief valve limits suction, and the gauge usually reads 4.5 to 5.5 inches of mercury [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. Vacuum or pressure systems often power the attitude and heading indicators while the electrical system powers the turn coordinator; most airplanes have at least two power sources so one source of bank information remains if the other fails [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]].

callout.text: Teach a habit of cross-checking instruments; when suction drops below normal the gyros can become unstable and inaccurate [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]].

check.q: In a climb, the airspeed slowly decays though pitch and power are normal. The altimeter has not moved for a minute. What is likely blocked, and what is the fix?
check.a: The static system: trapped static pressure freezes the altimeter and makes airspeed read low in a climb [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. Open the alternate static source [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

chunks.title: Environmental, ice protection, water rudders and oxygen

head: System
Facts
Teaching angle
rows: Environmental

Cabin heat in most light airplanes comes from air heated in a shroud around the muffler [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]]. Exhaust carries carbon monoxide, which is odorless and colorless, so the exhaust must be free of cracks [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]]. A defective exhaust heating system risks CO poisoning and fire [[1:189|PHAK 7-29]]. Pressurized airplanes typically hold about an 8,000 ft cabin [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]]
Show the heater shroud and exhaust on the walkaround; brief that you cannot smell CO
Deicing and anti-icing

Anti-icing prevents ice; deicing removes it [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]]. Most light airplanes have only a heated pitot tube and are not certified for icing; they must exit icing at once [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]]. Ice protection on a non-certified airplane is for emergency use only, and its stall warning will most likely not work in ice [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13]]
Teach that a heated pitot is not ice protection for the airplane
Water rudders
Seaplane equipment only (ACS AI.II.E.K1k is marked ASES, AMES)
Not tested in an ASEL airplane
Oxygen system

Required: crew above 12,500 ft cabin up to 14,000 ft for the part over 30 minutes; crew the whole time above 14,000 ft; every occupant provided oxygen above 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. Recommended: above 10,000 ft by day and 5,000 ft at night [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Preflight the mask, regulator, quantity and flow indicators, and keep oil and smoking away [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]

bullets: Deice boots: the old fear of ice bridging does not apply to modern boots; cycle them as soon as ice is seen, per the AFM/POH [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]].
Prop anti-ice: if a boot fails on one blade, unequal ice can cause severe vibration [[1:201|PHAK 7-41]]. Electric windshield heat can cause compass errors of up to 40 degrees [[1:201|PHAK 7-41]].
Check ice protection before you meet icing; the systems are not meant for long-term flight in ice [[1:201|PHAK 7-41]].
Oxygen: masks, not cannulas, are required for certified systems above 18,000 ft [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]. A pulse oximeter lets occupants check their own oxygen saturation [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

callout.text: Above a 15,000 ft cabin pressure altitude, every occupant must be provided supplemental oxygen [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(3)]].

check.q: Your student plans a mountain flight at a 13,500 ft cabin altitude for 50 minutes in a non-icing-certified airplane with pitot heat. Which systems questions do you ask?
check.a: Oxygen: the crew must use it for the 20 minutes beyond the first 30 at that altitude [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(1)]]. Icing: pitot heat does not make the airplane icing-capable, so plan to avoid and exit any icing [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]].

body.p: Procedures fall into three groups. Normal procedures are part of every flight. Abnormal procedures cover a system that is not working right but is not threatening, such as an electric trim failure secured by turning the trim switch off or pulling its breaker. Emergency procedures need a timely response: engine failure, fire, loss of pressurization, loss of a control system, or loss of instruments or avionics critical to the flight [[57:17|AC 90-109A para 8c(3)]].

head: Failure
Indications
Managing it
rows: Alternator
Ammeter discharge or low-voltage light [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]
Shed nonessential load, tell ATC, land at the nearest suitable airport; expect no flaps and a manual gear extension [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]
Electrical fire
Smell of burning insulation [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Find and isolate the circuit; if you cannot, master and alternator off. Land as soon as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Flaps will not extend
No flap movement
No-flap landing: up to 50 percent more runway and a wider, longer pattern; expect float, and do not force it on fast or flare excessively [[24:359|AFH 18-10]] [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]
Split flap
Strong roll toward the wing with less flap [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]
Opposite aileron and rudder, higher approach speed, no crosswind from the side of the extended flap [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]
Elevator cable
Yoke moves with no response in one direction [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]
Use trim plus the working direction of the yoke [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]
Abnormal engine indication
See Figure 18-11
Follow the AFM/POH; the AFH table gives generic causes and actions [[24:365|AFH 18-16]]

body.p: Detection is a scanning habit. Glance at the learner's eyes: a learner whose gaze never reaches the engine instruments may have an inattention problem, and one who stares at one instrument may be fixating [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Glass displays add a trap: failure indications are not standardized, and the primary and backup displays may react differently from each other and from round gauges [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

callout.text: Simulated failures carry real risk. Simulated engine failures done incorrectly have created real emergencies and accidents [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Brief the scenario, keep altitude and a landing option, and never disable a system you cannot restore at once.

check.q: An electric trim system fails in cruise. Is that an abnormal or an emergency procedure per AC 90-109A, and what is the generic action?
check.a: Abnormal: secure the system, for example trim switch off or trim breaker pulled; workload should rise only slightly [[57:17|AC 90-109A para 8c(3)(b)]].

chunks.title: Instructing in unfamiliar aircraft and avionics

body.p: This is a risk for the instructor, not just the student. Instructors should be familiar with aircraft, avionics and procedures; any unfamiliarity creates a hazard [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. An instructor should be thoroughly familiar with every instrument, avionics unit and system used for training, especially given the wide variety of GPS and glass panels [[25:165|AIH 8-7]]. Even highly experienced instructors face stress and risk when they meet a new system or avionics suite [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

bullets: Before you teach: familiarize yourself with the model and its avionics, from reviewing the POH or avionics manuals up to getting flight time in it [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].
Before teaching in advanced aircraft, make sure you know the aircraft and equipment, and build scenarios around automation management and workload [[25:189|AIH 10-5]].
Moving from one manufacturer's equipment to another should give pause and may call for more conservative planning, because formats are not standardized [[25:22|AIH 1-18]].
Unfamiliarity with the aircraft and its systems is a hazard with high risk potential, never a risk control [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]].
Use a structured transition: systems, normal, abnormal and emergency procedures, performance and limitations [[57:14|AC 90-109A para 8a]].
Check the airplane's real status: an instructor who does not maintain the airplane may not know of inoperative equipment, so review the discrepancy list first [[25:190|AIH 10-6]] [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

body.p: Your own habits can betray you. In an AIH study, learners and flight instructors solved weight and balance problems well with charts from their own airplane and poorly with charts from an unfamiliar one; their procedures had become automatic and tied to the familiar charts [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]. The same happens with switch positions and avionics menus.

Transition students also bring risks. Pilots moving to more advanced aircraft meet more complex systems and avionics and expanded abnormal and emergency procedures; pilots moving to lighter, slower aircraft meet less performance than they expect [[25:189|AIH 10-5]]. Professional pilots used to flying as a crew may not be used to single-pilot operation [[25:190|AIH 10-6]].

callout.text: Glass display failure modes are hard or impossible to simulate in the airplane, which limits training. Get equipment-specific information so you can interpret and respond to failures correctly [[24:365|AFH 18-16]].

check.q: A school asks you to teach in a new glass-cockpit airplane tomorrow. You have never used its avionics. What do the sources say to do first?
check.a: Familiarize yourself before instructing: at least review the POH and avionics manuals, and get flight time in it if needed [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]; unfamiliarity is a hazard [[25:190|AIH 10-6]].

chunks.title: How to teach it: a systems lesson flow

head: Phase (AIH)
What you do in a systems lesson
rows: Explanation
On the ground, give the objective and completion standard, cover safety, and invite questions [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Use the POH schematic and the flow method [[57:16|AC 90-109A para 8b(2)]]
Demonstration (instructor tells, instructor does)
Operate the system exactly the way the learner will, in the order you explained it, and explain any deviation at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Learner tells, instructor does
The learner talks you through the procedure, for example a split-master alternator check, while you operate it; misunderstandings surface before the learner is busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Learner tells, learner does
The learner says and does each step; you watch for errors and stay ready to take control [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Evaluation
Learner self-assessment first, then your assessment, compared in discussion [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]

bullets: Build from known to unknown and simple to complex, for example fixed-pitch power before constant-speed power [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Avoid jargon the learner does not know [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Promote a positive attitude toward checklists; at a minimum use them from the preflight to shutdown and securing [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].
Use scenarios that grow: a low-fuel scenario first discussed in the classroom, then flown at the home airport, then on a cross-country [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

Before any simulated failure, brief the positive exchange of flight controls: "You have the flight controls," "I have the flight controls," "You have the flight controls," with a visual check [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

callout.text: For the S1 element, pick systems you can operate and explain cleanly from the right seat, but be ready for any of them, since the examiner chooses (ACS AI.II.E.S1).

check.q: Why should your student extend the same amount of flap at the same point in every pattern?
check.a: Consistent flap use makes the go-around a preplanned, familiar sequence based on where the airplane is in the pattern [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Memorized, not understood
Recites the POH but cannot answer "what if" [[25:60|AIH 3-9]]
Teach the why and the flow; ask prediction questions [[25:61|AIH 3-10]] [[57:16|AC 90-109A para 8b(3)]]
Checklist recited, not checked
Fast verbal checklist with no eyes on the item [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]
Slow down and put the "check" back in checklist: confirm each item is actually done [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]
Rpm first on a power reduction
Manifold pressure rises as rpm comes back [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]]
Throttle first going down, propeller first going up [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]]
Partial carb heat
Rough engine, heat pushed back in [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Full heat until normal power returns [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Trimming to fly
Attitude changes made with the trim wheel
Attitude first, then trim [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]]
Mode confusion
Surprised when the autopilot does not capture or reverts to roll mode
Callouts and mode checks after every change [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]
Engine gauges never scanned
Learner's eyes never go to the engine instruments [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]
Point it out and build a scan habit [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]
Head-down during a failure
Heading and altitude wander while the learner reads
Fly first; be ready to take the controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]

callout.text: When a learner errs, ask why it happened and what would prevent it. Errors with radios, for instance, drop quickly once learners understand what each radio is for [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

check.q: In a glass-panel trainer the MFD fails. Where do the engine indications go?
check.a: Engine data such as the tachometer, normally on the MFD, is shown on the remaining screen with the PFD instruments [[1:215|PHAK 8-13]].

f1.caption: Figure 9-7. This comparison of steps in the teaching process, the demonstration-performance method, and the telling-and-doing technique highlights similarities as well as differences. The main difference in the telling-and-doing technique is the important transition, learner tells, instructor does, which occurs between the second and third step. (AIH 9-7)
f1.alt: A three-column table. Traditional Teaching Process: Preparation, Presentation, Application, Review and Evaluation. Demonstration-Performance Method: Explanation, Demonstration, Learner performance supervision, Evaluation. Telling-and-Doing Technique: Preparation; Instructor tells, Instructor does; a highlighted Learner tells, Instructor does; Learner tells, Learner does; Learner does, Instructor evaluates.

f2.caption: Figure 6-4. Airplane controls, movement, axes of rotation, and type of stability. (PHAK 6-3)
f2.alt: Cessna-type airplane with three colored axes: orange lateral axis for elevator pitch, green vertical axis for rudder yaw, blue longitudinal axis for aileron roll, with a table matching each control surface to its movement, axis and type of stability.

f3.caption: Figure 7-30 (lower half). Fuel-pump system. (PHAK 7-26; the part labels are removed for the labeling game)
f3.alt: Low-wing fuel-pump system drawing: left and right wing tanks feed a fuel selector valve; a line rises to a strainer bowl, then to an electric pump block beside an engine-driven pump, then to a carburetor at upper left. A primer with a pull knob is plumbed from the strainer area at right.

f4.caption: Figure 7-34. Electrical system schematic. (PHAK 7-32)
f4.alt: Light airplane wiring diagram: battery, battery contactor, split ALT/BAT master switch, alternator and control unit, low-voltage light, ammeter, starter, magnetos, and orange primary and avionics bus bars feeding circuit breakers for lights, flaps, pitot heat, radios and instruments.

f5.caption: Figure 2-22. Two similar flight decks equipped with the same information two different ways, analog and digital. What are they indicating? Chances are that the analog pilot will review the top display before the bottom display. Conversely, the digitally trained pilot will review the instrument panel on the bottom first. (PHAK 2-28)
f5.alt: Two cockpit panels of the same airplane type. Top: a round-gauge six pack with engine gauges, two VOR heads and an HSI. Bottom: a large primary flight display with airspeed and altitude tapes, attitude and heading, plus standby airspeed indicator and the same master and light switches.

f6.caption: Figure 18-11. Commonly experienced in-flight abnormal engine instrument indications, their possible causes, and corrective actions. (AFH 18-16)
f6.alt: A three-column table: Malfunction, Probable Cause, Corrective Action. Rows include loss of rpm or manifold pressure in cruise, high and low oil temperature and pressure, high and low cylinder head temperature, ammeter discharge, surging rpm, rough running engine and loss of fuel pressure.

f7.caption: Figure 8-1. Pitot-static system and instruments. (PHAK 8-2)
f7.alt: Cutaway pitot tube with ram air inlet, drain hole and heaters connected by a red line to the airspeed indicator; blue static lines from the static port and alternate static source to the airspeed indicator, VSI and altimeter.

scenario.title: Checkout for an airline pilot in his new single
scenario.setup: A local airline captain has bought a low-wing, fuel-injected single with a glass PFD and MFD, electric trim and a two-axis autopilot. He asks you, a new CFI, for a checkout. You have never flown this avionics suite. On the checkout flight, the trim runs nose-down by itself during the climb. Later, descending to the airport, the PFD shows you higher and faster than expected with a very shallow descent rate.

questions.q: Before you accept the job, what do the sources say about your own familiarity?
questions.a: Unfamiliarity with the aircraft, avionics or procedures creates a hazard [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. Familiarize yourself first, from reviewing the POH and avionics manuals to getting flight time in it [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: He has thousands of hours. What risk does the AIH flag for this kind of pilot, and how do you start the ground lesson?
questions.a: Pilots used to crew operation may not be used to flying single-pilot without their employer's support [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. Start with a structured transition: systems, procedures, performance and limits [[57:14|AC 90-109A para 8a]], taught with the flow method from the POH [[57:15|AC 90-109A para 8b]].

questions.q: In the climb the trim runs nose-down by itself. What kind of procedure is this, and what is the generic action?
questions.a: An abnormal procedure: secure the system, for example trim switch off or trim breaker pulled, then fly with a slight increase in workload [[57:17|AC 90-109A para 8c(3)(b)]]. Use the POH procedure for that airplane; pilots should know how to respond to a trim runaway [[24:344|AFH 17-10]].

questions.q: In the descent the displays say high, fast and descending slowly, though the airplane feels normal. What fits, and how do you confirm it?
questions.a: A partly blocked static system, which may not show until the descent [[24:363|AFH 18-14]] [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. Open the alternate static source while descending; if the readings move a lot, keep using it [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

questions.q: The standby instruments agree with the PFD. Does that prove the static system is fine?
questions.a: No. In many glass-cockpit light airplanes the backup instruments share the same pitot-static inputs, so both can be wrong together [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

questions.q: After landing, how do you run the debrief?
questions.a: Collaborative assessment: he assesses himself first, then you compare it with your assessment [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Ask why each error happened and what would prevent it [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

skills.do: The ACS asks you to "Operate at least three of the systems listed in K1a through K1l appropriately" (ACS AI.II.E.S1). There is no numeric tolerance: use the POH procedure. As a CFI applicant, expect to operate each system from the right seat while you explain it as you would to a student, for example flaps and trim, the propeller and mixture, the electrical system, the autopilot modes, or the alternate static source, and to say how you would teach and troubleshoot it.
skills.practice: Pick each system on your airplane and teach it to a friend using the flow method [[57:15|AC 90-109A para 8b]] and the telling-and-doing steps [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. In flight, narrate every mode change out loud [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]], and practice explaining one system abnormal from the AFH table without notes [[24:365|AFH 18-16]].

quiz.q: On the walkaround your student calls a small tab 'the trim.' It moves opposite its control surface automatically, and nothing in the cockpit adjusts it. What is it?
options: An antiservo tab, which trims the surface in flight
A balance tab, which lightens the control forces
A ground adjustable tab, bent to stop a skid
A servo tab that the autopilot moves directly
quiz.why: A balance tab moves automatically opposite its surface to lighten control forces; it is not a trim unless its linkage can be adjusted from the cockpit. An antiservo tab moves the same way as the stabilator trailing edge [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]].

quiz.q: Your trainer has a small fixed metal tab on the rudder with no cockpit control. How is it set?
options: In flight, by the pilot through a cable to the rudder pedals
On the ground, bent by trial and error until the cruise skid stops
Automatically, moving opposite the rudder to lighten pedal forces
By the autopilot servo, which moves it to hold the heading
quiz.why: A ground adjustable tab is a nonmovable metal tab on the rudder, bent one way or the other on the ground and adjusted by trial and error until the airplane no longer skids in normal cruise [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]] [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]].

quiz.q: Your airplane has rudder-aileron interconnect springs. Can you still slip it for landing?
options: No, the springs lock the rudder to the ailerons
Yes, the spring force can be overridden
Only with the flaps up
Only above maneuvering speed
quiz.why: The interconnect springs move the rudder with the ailerons, but their force can be overridden when it is necessary to slip [[1:153|PHAK 6-5]].

quiz.q: Right after a cold-weather start, oil pressure is in the green but the oil temperature gauge has not moved. What is the best interpretation?
options: Normal: oil temperature rises slowly after a cold start
The oil temperature probe has failed; shut down
The engine is low on oil and the pump is losing prime
The oil cooler is blocked by debris
quiz.why: There should be oil pressure during the start, but oil temperature changes slowly and may take several minutes to rise on a cold engine [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]] [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].

quiz.q: The fuel grade your engine requires is not available. What does the PHAK say?
options: Use the next lower grade and lean aggressively
Use the next higher grade, never a lower one
Use automobile gas if it has the same octane
Mix two lower grades to raise the octane
quiz.why: If the proper grade is not available, use the next higher grade; never use a lower grade, which can lead to detonation [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]].

quiz.q: Which statement about a voltage regulator is correct?
options: It holds alternator output a little above battery voltage, about 14 V for a 12 V battery
It converts the alternator's AC output to DC before it reaches the battery
It disconnects the battery during starting so the starter gets full power
It limits the load on each circuit breaker so no circuit can overheat
quiz.why: The regulator stabilizes alternator output, which should be higher than battery voltage, about 14 volts for a 12-volt battery, to keep it charged [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].

quiz.q: On the run-up, what suction does the PHAK give as the usual range for the vacuum system?
options: About 1.5 to 2.5 inches of mercury, at idle
About 10 to 12 inches of mercury
About 4.5 to 5.5 inches of mercury
About 25 to 30 inches of mercury
quiz.why: Suction for the instruments varies, but is usually between 4.5 and 5.5 inches of mercury; below the normal range the gyros may become unstable and inaccurate [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. Use the AFM/POH limits for your airplane.

quiz.q: Your airplane has no alternate static source, and the static ports are iced over. What last resort does the PHAK describe?
options: Fly faster, so ram air clears the ice from the ports
Break the VSI glass to let cabin static pressure in
Open a window, which vents fresh air into the static lines
Pull the static drain plug in flight from the cabin
quiz.why: Without an alternate static source, a way to introduce static pressure is to break the glass face of the VSI, which most likely renders the VSI inoperative [[1:205|PHAK 8-3]].

quiz.q: Why does the AFH say glass display failures need equipment-specific study?
options: They never happen in light airplanes, so there is little to learn
Failure indications are not standardized, and displays may react differently
They are easy to simulate in flight with a breaker, so ground study adds nothing
Every maker uses one standard red X, so one lesson covers all panels
quiz.why: Electronic system failure indications are not standardized, and the primary and backup displays may respond differently to the same interruption [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. The failure modes are hard or impossible to simulate in the airplane, so get equipment-specific information [[24:365|AFH 18-16]].

quiz.q: For best protection, above what cabin altitude does the PHAK encourage supplemental oxygen at night?
quiz.why: Pilots are encouraged to use supplemental oxygen above 10,000 ft cabin altitude by day and above 5,000 ft at night [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

final_quiz.q: On a preflight of a light-sport airplane, your student says the left aileron is broken because it barely moves down while the right goes far up. What should you teach?
options: Ground the airplane, since down travel must always equal up travel on any aileron
Some LSAs use highly differential ailerons by design; check free movement and direction
Adjust the cable tension yourself before flight so the travel evens out
Ignore the ailerons, since only the elevator needs a range of motion check
final_quiz.why: Some LSAs move the ailerons in a highly differential way, with little down aileron; the pilot should do a full range of motion check and verify direction [[24:344|AFH 17-10]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot plans to take his turbocharged single to FL 200 using a cannula from the certified oxygen system. What does the PHAK say?
options: Cannulas are fine at any altitude if the flow is set high enough
Certified systems above 18,000 ft need masks, not cannulas
Cannulas are approved up to FL 250 when a pulse oximeter is worn
Masks are needed only above FL 250, where every occupant needs oxygen
final_quiz.why: Airplanes with oxygen systems installed and certified for operations above 18,000 ft must be equipped with oxygen masks instead of cannulas [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]. A pulse oximeter lets occupants check their saturation but does not change that [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

final_quiz.q: In a fixed-pitch airplane you apply carb heat in cruise. The rpm drops and then stays constant. What does that tell you?
options: Ice was present and is melting
No carburetor ice was present
The carb heat valve has failed
The mixture is too lean
final_quiz.why: With ice present, rpm drops then gradually rises as the ice melts; if ice is not present, rpm drops and then remains constant [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

final_quiz.q: Oil pressure starts to fluctuate in cruise. Using AFH Figure 18-11, what is the corrective action listed?
options: Enrich the mixture and reduce power, then continue to the destination as planned
Adjust the cowl flaps to bring the oil temperature down
Land as soon as possible, or feather the propeller and stop the engine
Apply carburetor heat in case the induction is icing
final_quiz.why: Fluctuating oil pressure (low oil supply, loose lines, defective relief valve) carries the same action as the low oil pressure rows: land as soon as possible or feather the propeller and stop the engine [[24:365|AFH 18-16]].

final_quiz.q: Fuel pressure drops to zero in a low-wing airplane with an engine-driven pump. What does AFH Figure 18-11 list as the action?
options: Reduce power and land at the nearest airport
Turn on the boost pump and switch tanks
Enrich the mixture to full rich
Open the alternate air door
final_quiz.why: Loss of fuel pressure (engine-driven pump failure or no fuel): turn on boost pumps, switch tanks, turn on fuel [[24:365|AFH 18-16]].

final_quiz.q: Your student plans to run the left tank dry in cruise 'to use all the fuel' before switching. What does the PHAK warn?
options: Nothing; the engine restarts at once when the other tank is selected
Running a tank dry can let air into the lines and cause vapor lock
It is required, so the fuel gauges can be checked at the empty mark
It matters only in a high-wing airplane with gravity-feed tanks
final_quiz.why: Running a tank completely dry may allow air to enter the fuel system and cause vapor lock, which makes it difficult to restart the engine [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]].

final_quiz.q: On final you select flaps and the airplane rolls hard to the left. Which crosswind should you not land with?
options: A crosswind from the left
A crosswind from the right
Any headwind
None; crosswind does not matter
final_quiz.why: An asymmetric flap rolls the airplane toward the wing with less flap, so the right flap is the one extended. Do not land with a crosswind from the side of the deployed flap [[24:360|AFH 18-11]].

final_quiz.q: After the start, your student leaves the primer knob unlocked. Why does it matter?
options: It drains fuel from the tanks back into the cabin
It can vibrate out in flight and richen the mixture
It keeps the magnetos from grounding at shutdown
It lets carburetor ice form faster in the venturi
final_quiz.why: Lock the primer in place when not in use: if the knob is free to move, it may vibrate out during flight and cause an excessively rich mixture [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]].

final_quiz.q: Preflighting a retractable airplane, your student reaches for the master switch first thing. What should be confirmed before it goes on?
options: The fuel caps and oil, so the gauges read right at once
That the landing gear control is DOWN
That the gear motor breaker is pulled so the gear cannot move
The strobes, since they draw the most current at startup
final_quiz.why: The AFH cockpit preflight starts with the landing gear control DOWN (if applicable) and the master, alternator and magneto switches OFF [[24:42|AFH 2-5]].

final_quiz.q: Your student's checkout airplane has a castering nosewheel. How will she steer in tight turns while taxiing?
options: With the yoke, which turns the nosewheel through a linkage
With the rudder pedals alone, since the nosewheel is linked to them
With rudder and differential braking as needed
With the tow bar attached, since it cannot be steered under power
final_quiz.why: Castering nosewheels are free to swivel, and the pilot may need to combine rudder with independent use of the brakes to steer [[1:193|PHAK 7-33]] [[1:194|PHAK 7-34]].

final_quiz.q: Per AC 90-109A, roughly what share of fuel-related accidents came from fuel mismanagement?
options: About one-tenth, since most came from fuel contamination
Almost one-third
More than nine-tenths, nearly all of them
About one-half, the same share as fuel exhaustion
final_quiz.why: AC 90-109A notes that complex and high-performance airplanes may have complicated fuel systems, and that the 2009 Nall report found almost one-third of fuel-related accidents were a result of fuel mismanagement [[57:51|AC 90-109A App 10]].

final_quiz.q: With the electric windshield heat on, the magnetic compass disagrees with the heading indicator by 30 degrees. What is the likely cause?
options: A failed AHRS feeding the compass
Windshield heater current, which can cause compass errors of up to 40°
Carburetor ice, which is cutting the voltage to the compass light
A blocked static port, which tilts the compass card in level flight
final_quiz.why: Electric windscreen anti-ice current can cause compass deviation errors of as much as 40 degrees [[1:201|PHAK 7-41]].

final_quiz.q: Your student's new light-sport airplane has electric trim. Besides running the trim both ways, what does the AFH preflight add?
options: Running it full nose-down so the autopilot can set takeoff trim
Checking the trim disconnect and setting takeoff trim
Pulling the trim breaker, since electric trim may not be used on takeoff
Nothing more, since electric trim cannot run away in a light airplane
final_quiz.why: Preflight should include actuating the trim switch nose-up and nose-down, verifying the trim disconnect (if equipped) works, and setting takeoff trim; the pilot must also know how to respond to a trim runaway [[24:344|AFH 17-10]].

takeaways: The AFM/POH is the primary source for every system; teach students to open it first.
Teach systems as flows, from source to use, and ask "what if" questions to build understanding.
Know the indications: carb ice, blocked pitot or static, ammeter and loadmeter readings, and the AFH engine table.
Sort failures into normal, abnormal and emergency procedures, and always fly the airplane first.
Automation: know engaged and armed modes, call them out, and hand fly regularly.
Your unfamiliarity with an airplane or avionics suite is a hazard; familiarize before you teach.
Use telling-and-doing, positive exchange of controls, and collaborative debriefs for every systems lesson.
cfi_notes: PHAK 7-37 paraphrases the oxygen rule loosely: "flight crews", "between 12,500 and 14,000 feet", and every occupant above 15,000 ft must "have available" oxygen [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. 14 CFR 91.211 says the required minimum flight crew, above 12,500 ft up to and including 14,000 ft, for the part of the flight there of more than 30 minutes, and each occupant must be provided oxygen above 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. Teach the CFR wording.

AIH 5-21 counts five demonstration-performance phases [[25:124|AIH 5-21]] and AIH 9-5 counts four, with learner performance and instructor supervision as one [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Same method; FI.I.B and FI.I.C cover the difference.

AFH 18-13 says a 25 amp-hour battery at 10 amps might last only 2 hours, not the 2.5 hours simple division gives, because the higher the load, the faster the stored energy is used; an old battery or a late-detected failure leaves even less [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. Teach the conservative number.
PHAK 2-27 still says pilots must fly within the standards of the PTS [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]]; the current standard is the ACS. Teach the ACS.
Some older POHs and pilots still warn about ice bridging; the PHAK says it does not occur with modern boots, but the AFM/POH governs the airplane you fly [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]].

AC 90-109A is written with experimental and unfamiliar airplanes in mind, but its flow method works for any system on any airplane [[57:16|AC 90-109A para 8b(3)]]. It is the best single tool for a systems ground lesson.

Glass display failures are not standardized and are hard to simulate in flight [[24:364|AFH 18-15]] [[24:365|AFH 18-16]]. Use the avionics maker's training software or a simulator for failure training, as the AIH suggests for both instructor and learner [[25:22|AIH 1-18]].

Never simulate a failure you cannot undo at once. Simulated engine failures done incorrectly have caused real emergencies and accidents [[25:191|AIH 10-7]], and turning off the alternator side of the master puts the whole load on the battery [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].
On the checkride, bring the POH tabbed at the systems section and the emergency and abnormal procedures; the examiner tests the airplane provided (ACS AI.II.E objective).
gaps: Allowed mag drop, normal suction range, ammeter limits, flap speeds and emergency gear extension steps for your airplane come only from its AFM/POH.
No source gives a safe, approved way to simulate specific system failures in flight (which breakers to pull, which switches to turn off); use the AFM/POH and your school's procedures.
The sources do not say which three systems an examiner will choose for S1; be ready for any of them.
Avionics failure modes and autopilot mode logic vary by manufacturer and are not standardized; the avionics pilot's guide or AFM supplement is needed.
The handbooks do not cover carbon monoxide detectors or their use; check the airplane's equipment and the AFM/POH.
Water rudders (K1k) are seaplane equipment and are not covered for an ASEL airplane.

activities.title: True or false: controls and trim
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Adverse yaw is strongest at high airspeed.
cards.why: False. It becomes more pronounced at low airspeeds, where larger aileron inputs are needed [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]] [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]].

cards.s: Turning the control wheel to the right raises the right aileron.
cards.why: True. The right aileron deflects up and the left one down, so the airplane rolls right [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]].

cards.s: Spoilers used for roll control eliminate adverse yaw.
cards.why: True. An advantage of spoilers for roll control is the elimination of adverse yaw [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]].

cards.s: A balance tab moves in the same direction as its control surface.
cards.why: False. A balance tab automatically moves opposite to the surface; the antiservo tab is the one that moves the same way [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]].

cards.s: The rudder becomes less effective as airspeed increases.
cards.why: False. Rudder effectiveness increases with speed, so small inputs suffice at high speed [[1:156|PHAK 6-8]].

cards.s: Normal technique is to set power, attitude and configuration first, then trim.
cards.why: True. Establish them first, then trim to relieve control pressure [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]].

activities.title: Work the systems numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: The outside air is 100 degrees F and the carburetor causes a 70 Fahrenheit-degree drop. What is the air temperature in the carburetor?
items.why: 100 - 70 = 30 degrees F, cold enough for ice [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]] [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

items.q: Convert that 70 Fahrenheit-degree drop into Celsius degrees (180 F degrees equal 100 C degrees).
After an alternator failure, a 25 amp-hour battery carries a 5 amp load. How many hours does the AFH say it could last?
items.why: 25 amp-hours / 5 amps = 5 hours, if the battery is in good condition [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

items.q: Your normal landing distance is 1,200 ft. The flaps fail. Using the AFH's figure for the most extra distance, how much runway might you need?
You cruise 40 minutes at a 13,000 ft cabin altitude, then 15 minutes at 14,500 ft. For how many minutes in all must the required minimum flight crew use oxygen?
items.why: From 12,500 ft up to and including 14,000 ft, the crew uses oxygen for the part over 30 minutes (40 - 30 = 10), and above 14,000 ft for the whole time (15): 10 + 15 = 25 minutes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(1)]] [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(2)]].

activities.title: Isolate an electrical fire
activities.intro: Electrical power is essential and you smell burning insulation. Put the AFH steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Turn the electrical master switch OFF
Turn all individual electrical switches OFF
Turn the master switch back ON
Turn the switches that were on back on one at a time, pausing after each to check for odor, smoke or sparks

activities.title: A systems lesson, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are giving a systems lesson to a student pilot in the school's carbureted, fixed-pitch trainer, from the preflight to the debrief.

steps.s: On the preflight your student skips the POH checklist, saying it is "just for beginners", and walks past the control lock.
options: Let it go; experienced pilots fly from memory
Stop and use the checklist; the control lock must be removed, and checklists exist because crews took off with locked controls
Remove the lock yourself and say nothing
Cancel the lesson
steps.why: Control column locks removed is a preflight item [[24:42|AFH 2-5]], and accidents with locked controls are why checklists are used in every airplane [[57:16|AC 90-109A para 8c]]. Promote a positive attitude toward checklists [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

steps.s: On the run-up the suction gauge reads well below its normal range.
options: Fly; the attitude indicator looks fine on the ground
Do not depart; with low suction the gyros may be unreliable, so have it checked
Use more rpm in flight to fix it
Ignore it; the turn coordinator is vacuum powered too
steps.why: When suction is below the normal range the attitude and heading indicators may be unstable and inaccurate [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. Check the AFM/POH limits.

steps.s: In cruise you ask her to lean. She pulls the mixture until the engine roughens and leaves it there.
options: Praise her; rough means lean enough
Have her enrich until smooth and use the AFM/POH leaning procedure, because too lean can cause detonation
Tell her to go full rich for the rest of the flight
Apply carb heat
steps.why: An overly lean mixture can cause detonation, roughness, overheating or power loss, and the leaning procedure varies by airplane, so use the AFM/POH [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

steps.s: You simulate a rough engine. She goes head-down into the checklist, and the heading wanders 30 degrees as the nose drops.
options: Let her keep reading until she finishes
Coach her to fly the airplane first, guard the controls, and be ready to take over if it gets worse
Grab the controls without saying anything
End the simulation and return home
steps.why: Be ready to take control at any time [[25:178|AIH 9-8]], allowing time and space to take over before the situation deteriorates [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. In an emergency the first priority is to fly the aircraft [[25:29|AIH 1-25]].

steps.s: Back on the ground she asks why the run-up includes a carburetor heat check.
options: To melt ice that formed during taxi, so the takeoff is ice free
To confirm the carb heat works before you need it in flight
To lean the mixture for takeoff, since heat enriches it
It is not needed at all in a fixed-pitch airplane
steps.why: The carburetor heat should be checked during the engine runup, following the manufacturer's recommendations, so it is known to work before carburetor icing conditions are met in flight [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
